docs.title: chora
docs.text:
chora is the space where forms appear.

chora is a Wayland compositor without policy. It is a programmable scene, not a desktop.

chora has no window manager, no layout, no keybindings and no look. The core renders a small scene of primitives and offers one API. Plugins add all other behavior. A plugin can supply a stacking desktop, a tiling workflow, or a view that an agent arranges live by voice. Only a small safety layer is built in.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Early development. chora runs nested inside another Wayland session, and a reference plugin tiles the windows. A login session on real hardware exists, but nobody tested it on hardware yet. An agent sees and changes the screen through choractl mcp, after a grant of the user. The roadmap shows the next steps. APIs change without notice before version 1.0.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Each release has an RPM for Fedora 44, with SHA256 sums:

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
sudo dnf install ./chora-*.rpm

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Start chora with the tiling plugin inside a Wayland session:

chora -- chora-tiling

A window opens. The plugin uses these bindings:

Binding Action Super+Return start a terminal (foot) Super+d start a launcher (fuzzel) Super+q close the focused window Super+j, Super+k focus the next or previous window

GNOME keeps Super for itself. There, start chora -- chora-tiling --mod alt to use Alt instead. chora-tiling --help lists all options.

The safety layer has two fixed bindings: Ctrl+Alt+Escape resets the scene, and Ctrl+Alt+BackSpace quits chora.

To let an agent drive chora, grant it screenshots and input, and add choractl --name agent mcp as an MCP server of the agent:

choractl grant agent screen.capture input.inject

The agent can then put its own shaders and images, reserve a panel at the edge of the output, wait for clicks and keys, and move the camera. With choractl grant agent process.spawn, it can also start programs and restart plugins.

To try the XP flavor, a stacking desktop in the style of Windows XP, start chora -- chora-xp. From a source tree, point it at the theme: target/debug/chora -- target/debug/chora-xp --theme flavors/xp/theme. Windows wobble while you drag them and minimize through a magic lamp. Ctrl+Alt+Left and Ctrl+Alt+Right, or the desktop buttons 1 to 4 in the taskbar, turn a cube of four desktops. Inside GNOME, which keeps Ctrl+Alt+arrows and Super for itself, use the desktop buttons and the start menu.

To log in to chora on real hardware, choose the session "chora" on the login screen. It starts the tiling flavor with waybar and X11 support through xwayland-satellite. The session "chora (Windows XP)" starts the XP flavor. The hardware session is not tested yet.

Programs inside chora find its IPC socket in CHORA_SOCKET. For example, a terminal in chora shows the scene with choractl query, and choractl events prints the events.

docs.title: Compositors
docs.text:
Project Stack Extension model Fit for chora Missing River 0.4 Zig, wlroots the window manager is a separate process; it speaks the stable river-window-management-v1 protocol with atomic, frame-perfect updates closest to "the window manager is a plugin" no scene graph, no shaders or effects Pinnacle Rust, Smithay gRPC API with Lua and Rust clients; Snowcap widgets a Rust base with an external API; the layout runs in a client policy in the core (tags, layout modes, window rules), no scene graph, no shaders, no MCP; small team niri Rust, Smithay KDL config, niri msg IPC, no plugins best Smithay reference for rendering, shaders, blur and animations scrolling tiling is built in cosmic-comp Rust, Smithay none production-grade Smithay reference bound to COSMIC Jay Rust, own stack config as a Rust library (unverified) reference for a Vulkan renderer not Smithay Wayfire C++, wlroots in-process C++ plugins, IPC close plugin idea, 3D effects unsafe C++ ABI, slow releases Hyprland C++, Aquamarine C++ plugins with an unstable ABI, Lua config the target effects opinionated; the plugin ABI breaks with every release Mir and MirAL C++ libraries for shells mature C++; the policy model of MirAL Louvre C++ library with replaceable defaults good scene API not Rust scenefx C, wlroots wlroots scene with blur, shadows and rounded corners scene graph and effects C and wlroots only CwC, SomeWM, Strata C and Lua, Rust and Lua scripted configs scriptable no policy-free core with a scene graph

Agent tools exist today only as external MCP servers on top of existing compositors, for example kwin-mcp, and hypruse for Hyprland. The check found no compositor with an MCP interface of its own. The combination of chora appears to be new: a policy-free core, a scene of primitives with shaders, and one API for plugins and agents.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Build on Smithay and copy from others. Sources: the anvil and smallvil examples, niri, cosmic-comp, Pinnacle. This option gives full control of the scene and the plugin model. This is the decision (D15).
  2. Fork Pinnacle. A working Smithay compositor with an external API on day one. The code review below rejects this option.
  3. River 0.4 with a Rust window manager. No compositor code, but no shaders, no effects and no scene. This option drops the game-engine half of the idea. It is a fallback for a quick tiling prototype.
  4. An MCP server on an existing compositor, like kwin-mcp. This is the fastest way to try agentic workflows. It gives no canvas and no effects.

River shows a strong design for the window manager interface. chora can copy its semantics without its code.

docs.title: Pinnacle code review
docs.text:
The review measured a clone of Pinnacle 0.2.2 (last commit 2026-06-27).

  • Size: 34,138 lines of Rust in src/. The workspace adds the client API (Rust and Lua), the Snowcap widget toolkit and a wlcs test adapter.
  • Policy in the core: tags touch 20 files, layout modes 20 files, window rules 8 files. Click-to-focus is hardcoded.
  • Rendering: a flat list of Smithay render elements on top of Smithay's Space. No scene graph and no custom shaders. Space appears in 23 files.
  • API: tonic gRPC with 115 methods around tags and layout modes. No batching and no transactions for clients.
  • Transactions: yes, for window positions per output. A transaction completes when every window commits, or after 150 ms. The design comes from niri.
  • License: GPL-3.0-or-later. src/protocol/drm.rs is GPL-3.0-only. The API crates and Snowcap are MPL-2.0.
  • Activity: 57 commits in February 2026, then 2, 3 and 8 per month.

A fork keeps about 40 to 50 percent of src/. It deletes or rewrites the spine that chora replaces: Space, the window state, tags and the API. Only the generic parts survive, and these are easy to copy. Dependencies lists them.

docs.title: Plugin runtimes
docs.text:
Runtime Strengths Weaknesses Extism on wasmtime more than 13 guest languages, simple, sandboxed bytes in, bytes out: every call serializes and copies wasmtime with the Component Model typed WIT interfaces, handles to scene nodes, fuel and epoch limits, fast new instances fewer mature guest languages; Rust is first-class wasmer works less momentum for the Component Model mlua with LuaJIT or Luau low friction, easy reload, Luau sandbox no memory isolation from the host Rhai pure Rust, easy slow tree-walking interpreter Rune native to Rust not at 1.0 deno_core (V8) JS and TS ecosystem heavy, GC pauses, API churn abi_stable dylibs native speed stale, unsafe unloading, no sandbox IPC clients (separate processes) any language, crash isolation from the OS, no runtime in the core a round trip per event; no code in every frame

For code in every frame, the Component Model is better than Extism. Typed calls only help when the boundary stays typed: JSON over WIT gives back the cost of Extism. chora starts with IPC clients only (D28). wasmtime comes when a measurement demands it.

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
• niri, cosmic-comp and Pinnacle use the GLES renderer of Smithay. Custom GLSL shaders through texture and pixel shader elements work in practice, for example the blur of niri.
  • No Smithay compositor renders through wgpu. The Smithay maintainers consider wgpu too abstract for a compositor. Smithay has no merged Vulkan renderer either.
  • Decision: GLES and GLSL (D17).

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: rmcp 3.x supports stdio and Streamable HTTP. choractl mcp uses stdio. A container gets the socket through a bind mount, so chora needs no network transport for now.

docs.title: Widgets and shells
docs.text:
Quickshell is the strongest choice: Qt6 and QML, declarative, with live reload. waybar is mature. eww and AGS/Astal need a check of their activity. All of these need wlr-layer-shell.

For HTML from agents, a browser in app mode (chromium --app=...) is enough (D38). chora places toplevels anywhere. A dedicated host on gtk4-layer-shell with WebKitGTK, or a Tauri window as a layer surface, is an option for later.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Draft

A first sketch of the one API of chora. Names and shapes will change. The principle stays: plugins, choractl and agents use one language of commands and events.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A command changes the scene. An event reports a change. Commands travel in transactions (see Architecture). Ownership decides who may change a node.

# one transaction
- create: {id: work, kind: group, parent: root}
- create: {id: bar, kind: rect, parent: work, props: {size: [1280, 30], color: [0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1]}}
- attach: {surface: s42, parent: work}
- configure: {surface: s42, size: [900, 600], states: [activated]}
- update: {id: s42, props: {transform: {translate: [40, 40]}}}
- focus: {surface: s42}

create and update take the node properties in props. Unknown fields are errors, so a typo never passes silently.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
This table is the one list of node properties.

Property Nodes Meaning id all stable id; ids of the form s1, s2 belong to surfaces, and the core assigns them owner all client name of the owner; read-only transform all a 4x4 matrix, or the short form translate, scale, rotate opacity, visible all clip group, rect, image, shader {"radius": r}: the node and its descendants show only inside its size, with corners rounded by r logical pixels, and take pointer input only there; the node becomes a layer; null removes the clip effects group, rect, image up to 8 effects {"shader": path, "uniforms": {name: number or 2 to 4 numbers}}; the node becomes a layer, and the core applies the shaders in order; [] removes them input all accept, pass or block; pass and block apply to all descendants meta all free key/value pairs to tag and find nodes size group, rect, image, shader width and height; an image without a size has the size of its file; for a group, the area of its layer mesh group, rect, image cols and rows from 1 to 64, and points: the place of each grid point in node coordinates, row by row from the top left; the node becomes a layer that shows through the grid; points: [] removes the mesh color rect RGBA, each from 0 to 1 radius rect the radius of the corners in logical pixels; the rect becomes a layer border rect {"width": w, "color": [r, g, b, a]}: a line of w logical pixels along the inner edge; the rect becomes a layer; null removes it image image absolute path of a PNG file; the core loads it again after a change slice image insets left, top, right, bottom in pixels of the file: the corners keep their size, the edges and the center stretch shader, uniforms shader the absolute path of a GLSL ES fragment shader, and its uniforms as for an effect; a uniform {"node": id} is a sampler2D with that node as it shows on its own, at most 4

A surface node gets its size from its client. The configure command asks the client for a new size.

A shader node draws its shader over its size, as a layer. Its children render into uniform sampler2D tex, and the shader gets the same inputs as an effect. A node texture shows the node without its transform, at its size or, for a surface, at the size of the window. A node with opacity 0 hides in the scene and still shows in a node texture. Inside a node texture, shader nodes get no node textures of their own, so that two shader nodes that read each other do not recurse.

# a rounded button with a border, a round clip and a shader that reads it
- create: {id: button, kind: rect, parent: root, props: {size: [120, 40], color: [0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1], radius: 8, border: {width: 2, color: [1, 1, 1, 1]}}}
- create: {id: avatar, kind: group, parent: root, props: {size: [64, 64], clip: {radius: 32}}}
- create: {id: glow, kind: shader, parent: root, props: {size: [400, 300], shader: /home/me/glow.frag, uniforms: {strength: 0.5, picture: {node: avatar}}}}
- update: {id: button, props: {border: null}}

A node with a size and a mesh, or with a transform that is not a plain 2D translation and scale, for example a rotation or a perspective, is a layer (see Architecture). animate moves the points of a mesh of the same grid, for example for a magic lamp minimize.

An effect is a GLSL ES fragment shader with absolute path. It reads the layer in uniform sampler2D tex at varying vec2 v_uv, and may use uniform float alpha, uniform vec2 size (the texture size in pixels), uniform float time (seconds) and its own float and vec2 to vec4 uniforms. A transaction that names a shader that does not compile fails with the log of the compiler. The core compiles a shader again when its file changes. The package installs examples in /usr/share/chora/shaders/: grayscale.frag, rounded.frag and blur.frag (with radius).

The core loads the file of an image when a transaction names it. A file that does not load, that is larger than 32 MiB or larger than 8192 pixels on a side rejects the transaction. A plugin in a container shares its asset directory with the core, as it shares the socket directory.

A client that shares no directory with the core, for example an agent in another container, hands its files to the core with assets.put (#6). The core stores them in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora/ and answers with the absolute path for image, shader and effects. A file has at most 512 KiB, a client at most 64 files, all clients together at most 64 MiB. A second put of a name replaces the file, and the nodes that use it load it again. The files of a client go with its nodes: at the last disconnect without keep_nodes, otherwise when chora exits. choractl asset put NAME FILE prints the path.

docs.title: Commands
Selectors
docs.text: A selector finds nodes: id:work, kind:surface, owner:tiling, app_id:firefox, title:"make test" (exact), title~:Inbox (contains), meta:role=editor. Conditions separated by spaces must all match. A value with spaces goes in double quotes. An empty selector or * matches every node. Selectors work in queries only. A query returns all current matches, or an empty list. It always sees the current titles.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Data surface.created a toplevel waits for a plugin: surface id, app_id, title, and decoration: server when the client asked for a frame of the plugins through xdg-decoration, client when it draws its own surface.changed surface id, app_id, title, size and decoration, after any of them changed surface.destroyed, surface.detached surface id; surface.destroyed follows only a surface.created surface.requested surface id and request: activate, close, fullscreen, unfullscreen, maximize, unmaximize or minimize; a client or a taskbar asks, and plugins decide input.key the grabbed binding pointer.entered, pointer.left the pointer came over or left the top node under it that takes input: node; not during a drag of a node or while locked pointer.pressed a button went down over a node that takes input: node, Linux button code, position in scene coordinates pointer.moved, pointer.released after a press over a rect or an image, until the button goes up: node and position; pointer.released with the button animation.done the node whose animation reached its targets, or the output whose camera did effect.failed the shader of an effect failed after a change of its file: path and log; the effect keeps its last working version effects.dropped the watchdog removed the effects, the meshes and the shaders of shader nodes of all nodes, because frames were slow for two seconds output.changed output name, layout position and size, scale, camera, and the work area: the scene area that the output shows without panels and reserves output.removed output name client.connected, client.disconnected client name method.called another client calls a method that this connection exported: call id, caller, method and params; only the exporting connection gets it, subscribed or not

The response of scene.apply reports the result of a transaction: null when it applied, an error with the index of the failed command when not. A request that a client makes before its first commit follows its surface.created. A taskbar asks through wlr-foreign-toplevel-management. The core does not act on a request, also not on close. A plugin answers with commands, for example close. A press over a surface reaches its client as well; a press over a rect or an image goes to plugins only, with the moves and the release that follow, so that a plugin can drag a window by its title bar. Later milestones add events for size limits.

docs.title: IPC methods
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line, on the socket in CHORA_SOCKET. Every client sends hello first. The core answers every request.

Method Purpose hello(name, keep_nodes) name the client; keep_nodes keeps its nodes and cameras after the disconnect scene.query(selector) read nodes scene.apply(commands) apply a transaction events.subscribe(events) stream the named events, or all events for an empty list, as notifications input.grab(binding) get the events of a key, a button or a gesture; returns the binding as input.key names it input.inject(events) send synthetic input: pointer, buttons, scrolling, keys, shortcuts and text; needs a grant screen.capture(output, node, max_side) capture an output or a node as a PNG file; needs a grant grants.set(client, capabilities), grants.revoke(client, capabilities), grants.list grant or revoke input.inject, screen.capture and process.spawn for a client name; choractl grant and choractl revoke call them output.list list the outputs and their cameras output.reserve(output, edges) leave space at the edges of an output out of its work area while the connection lives, as the exclusive zone of a panel does; edges has top, right, bottom and left in logical pixels, and no space removes the reserve; returns the output clients.list list the connected client names and the methods that each exported methods.export(names) offer methods of this client to other clients methods.call(client, method, params) call a method of another client; the answer is the result of the method methods.return(call, result, error) answer a method.called event process.spawn(argv) start a program with the environment of the core; needs the grant process.spawn plugins.restart(name) stop the process of a client name and start its command again; needs the grant process.spawn assets.put(name, data) store a file in base64 for image nodes, shader nodes and effects; returns its path assets.remove(name) remove a file of assets.put

A connection sends hello once, within 5 s. Connections with the same name share their nodes, so they must agree on keep_nodes. The core refuses a hello with a different value. For example, choractl --name tiling fails while the tiling plugin runs.

A reserve of output.reserve belongs to a connection and ends with it, also when its client crashes (#8). The reserves of all connections on an output add up, and count from the edges of the area that the exclusive zones of layer surfaces leave free. At least one pixel of the work area stays. choractl reserve --top 30 holds a reserve until it ends.

A key binding needs Ctrl, Alt or Super, so that typing still works. The bindings of the safety layer, Ctrl+Alt with BackSpace, Escape or F1 to F12, belong to no client. A binding has one owner at a time.

The core implements wlr-output-management, so kanshi and wlr-randr configure the outputs (see Architecture). The API has no output configuration of its own. After a new mode, position, transform or scale, the core sends output.changed. For an output that turns off, it sends output.removed, and output.list no longer lists the output.

docs.title: Grants
docs.text:
input.inject and screen.capture see or drive the whole session, and process.spawn runs any program as the user, so they need a grant of the user for the client name (D40, D42):

$ choractl grant agent screen.capture input.inject
$ choractl grants
{"agent": ["input.inject", "screen.capture"]}
$ choractl revoke agent

A grant lasts until choractl revoke or the end of the session. The emergency reset revokes all grants. A grant protects against mistakes of agents, not against hostile code of the same user, which can call grants.set itself. choractl mcp offers no tool for grants.

docs.title: Programs
docs.text:
process.spawn(argv) starts a program with the environment of the core, as the startup command (D30): WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET of this compositor, without the variables of a host session, and with no stdin. The core looks the program up in its own PATH, so it works for an agent in another namespace too. The answer has the pid and the argv.

plugins.restart(name) restarts a plugin, for example after a rebuild (#9). The core finds the process of the connections of the client name, reads its command line and working directory from /proc, and sends it SIGTERM. Once it exited, or 5 s after a SIGKILL, the core starts the same command again and answers with the new pid. A name with several processes, or a process in a namespace that the core cannot see, fails.

Both methods need the grant process.spawn, and fail while the session is locked:

$ choractl grant agent process.spawn
$ choractl --name agent spawn foot
$ choractl --name agent restart tiling

A later version may narrow the grant with a list of allowed programs, which choractl grant reads from a file (D42).

docs.title: Screen capture
docs.text:
screen.capture renders an output, or a node with its descendants, and answers with a PNG file in base64:

Parameter Meaning output the output name; the first output if neither output nor node is set node a node id, for example a surface or a group max_side shrink the picture until its longer side has at most this many pixels

The result has the width and height in pixels, the scale in pixels per logical pixel, the origin and the png. A pixel at (px, py) shows the point origin + (px, py) / scale: in the logical coordinates of the output, whose origin is (0, 0), or in the coordinates of the node.

  • An output shows as on screen, without the cursor.
  • A node shows without its own transform, opacity, mesh and effects, on a transparent background, but with its rounded corners, border, clip and the shader of a shader node. Its area covers the descendants with a size.
  • A picture has at most 16 Mi pixels and 8192 pixels a side; a larger one shrinks. max_side must be at least 1.
  • A capture fails while the session is locked, and when the PNG file is larger than 5 MiB; a smaller max_side helps then.

choractl capture FILE saves a picture, for example choractl --name agent capture --node s1 window.png.

docs.title: Input injection
docs.text:
input.inject sends a list of events as one request:

{"events": [
  {"pointer_move": {"position": [640, 400], "output": "DP-1"}},
  {"click": {"button": 272}},
  {"text": {"text": "make test\n"}},
  {"shortcut": {"keys": "Super+Return"}}
]}
Event Fields pointer_move position in the logical coordinates of the output, as in a capture; output, the first one by default button button, a Linux code, 272 (left) by default; state: pressed or released click button; presses and releases it scroll dx and dy in logical pixels; a positive dy scrolls down key key: a keysym name such as Return, or a Linux key code such as 28; state shortcut keys, a binding such as Ctrl+Shift+t: the modifiers go down, the key goes down and up, the modifiers go up text text; a newline presses Return, a tab presses Tab
  • The core checks all events before the first one runs. An event that does not resolve, for example a character without a key, rejects the request.
  • Key names and text use the first layout of the keymap. A character needs a key with Shift or AltGr at most.
  • Keys and buttons that the events leave down go up at the end of the request, so that no key sticks.
  • Injected keys never reach the safety layer: Ctrl+Alt+BackSpace, Ctrl+Alt+Escape and the VT switch do nothing. The grabs of plugins see them, and the focused surface gets the rest.
  • A request has at most 256 events, 4096 characters of text in all and 32,768 steps, a key press and a release being two. It fails while the session is locked.

choractl inject reads the list of events as JSON, for example echo '[{"text": {"text": "ls\n"}}]' | choractl --name agent inject.

docs.title: Plugin methods
docs.text:
A plugin exports methods, and other clients call them by the client name and the method name, for example tiling.set_layout:

$ choractl call tiling set_layout '{"layout": "columns"}'
{"gap": 4, "layout": "columns", "windows": ["s1", "s2"]}

The core sends the exporting connection a method.called event. The plugin answers with methods.return: the same call and a result, or an error with a code and a message. The core passes the answer to the caller. The Client of chora-scene answers with Client::answer.

  • A method name has at most 64 characters: lowercase letters, digits, _, - and ., starting with a letter.
  • A connection exports at most 64 methods. Another connection of the same client name cannot export the same method.
  • A call without an answer fails after 10 s, and so does a call whose exporter disconnects. A connection has at most 64 calls in flight, and it cannot call its own methods.

chora-tiling exports two methods:

Method Parameters Result set_layout layout: master_stack, columns or rows; gap in logical pixels; a missing field keeps its value the layout, the gap and the tiled windows get_layout none the same

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
A plugin is a client with a manifest:

name: tiling
exec: chora-tiling
configure: set_layout

choractl view load reads the manifest of each plugin of a view: it starts a plugin that does not run with exec, and passes the config of the view to the method in configure (see Configuration). A flavor starts its plugins as systemd units instead.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text:
choractl mcp serves the API as MCP tools over stdio (D34). It connects as the client agent, or under --name. An MCP client starts it, for example in the .mcp.json of Claude Code:

{"mcpServers": {"chora": {"command": "choractl", "args": ["--name", "agent", "mcp"]}}}
Tool Purpose describe_screen a screenshot of an output, at most 1280 pixels a side by default, and in words: the outputs, the windows with their positions in scene coordinates and sizes, and the plugins with their methods capture a picture of an output or of a node, as screen.capture, at most 1920 pixels a side by default query_scene the nodes of a selector apply_commands a transaction list_plugins the connected clients and their methods call_method a method of a plugin, for example tiling.set_layout inject_input synthetic input, as input.inject load_view, save_view, unload_view the views of Configuration, by name only spawn_process, restart_plugin start a program, or restart a plugin, as process.spawn and plugins.restart reserve_space space at the edges of an output, as output.reserve, while the server runs put_asset a file for image nodes, shader nodes and effects, as assets.put: name, and text for a shader or base64 for a PNG; returns the path subscribe_events start to collect events, and grab keys (#7); events and keys as in events.subscribe and input.grab; replaces the earlier subscription wait_events the collected events: waits up to timeout_ms (5000 by default, at most 30000) for the first one, and returns at most max (50 by default, at most 500)

The input schemas of apply_commands and inject_input come from the types of chora-scene (#5). They list every command, every input event and every field, with its description, so the model sees the shape of a call before the first try. A test checks that the schemas, the types and the examples of this page agree.

The screenshot of describe_screen, capture, inject_input, spawn_process and restart_plugin need the grants of the client name, for example choractl grant agent screen.capture. Without a grant, describe_screen still describes the scene. No tool grants anything (D40).

A subscription has a connection of its own under the same client name. A thread reads its events into a buffer of 1000 events, so the core never waits for the agent. When the buffer is full, the oldest events go, and wait_events counts them in dropped. The grabs of the keys end with the subscription.

A tool that fails, also on invalid arguments, answers with isError and the reason, so that the model can correct its call. An unknown tool is a JSON-RPC error.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph core["chora (Rust, Smithay)"]
        protocols["Wayland protocols"]
        backends["Backends: DRM/KMS and libinput, winit for development"]
        scene["Scene: group, surface, rect, image, shader"]
        render["Renderer: GLES and GLSL shaders"]
        input["Input router"]
        ipc["IPC socket: JSON-RPC"]
        safety["Safety layer"]
    end
    clients["Wayland clients: apps, Quickshell, waybar, browsers"] <--> protocols
    plugins["Plugins: WM, layouts, keybindings"] <--> ipc
    choractl["choractl: CLI and MCP bridge"] <--> ipc
    services["Services in containers"] <--> ipc
    agents["Agents: MCP clients"] <--> choractl
    services -.-> clients
    plugins -.-> clients

The core has one language: commands and events (see API). Plugins, choractl, services and agents all use it. Nothing outside the core changes the scene in another way.

Plugins are separate processes (D28). A plugin can also be a Wayland client, for example to draw window decorations as its own surfaces.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
The compositor binary chora. Its tasks, and nothing more:

  • Wayland protocol handling and the client lifecycle, through Smithay.
  • Backends: DRM/KMS and libinput on real hardware, through libseat. A winit window for development inside another compositor. chora uses winit when WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY is set, and the hardware otherwise. On hardware it draws the cursor of the xcursor theme in XCURSOR_THEME.
  • The scene, rendered every frame.
  • Input routing (see below).
  • The IPC socket.
  • The safety layer (see below).
  • The startup command: chora -- <command> runs one command with WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET set. The command does not get the variables that reach a host compositor, for example WAYLAND_SOCKET and SWAYSOCK. Without a command, the core shows a black screen.

The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces itself, because the protocols define their position. Smithay's PopupManager and LayerMap do this work. Layer surfaces, for example panels and launchers, sit in the coordinates of their output, outside its camera, so a panel stays in place when a plugin pans the scene. The background and bottom layers are below the scene, the top and overlay layers above it. A panel reserves an exclusive zone, and an IPC client reserves space with output.reserve; the rest of the output is its work area. Only toplevels wait for a plugin: the core creates a detached surface node and sends surface.created. A plugin decides where the surface appears, or if it appears at all.

Taskbars see the toplevels through ext-foreign-toplevel-list and wlr-foreign-toplevel-management. A handle of the second protocol reports the title, the application id and the outputs that show the surface. Its states are activated for the surface that plugins focused, and maximized and fullscreen from the last configure. The core never reports minimized. The requests of a taskbar, close included, go to plugins as surface.requested.

Screenshot tools and screen sharing capture outputs through wlr-screencopy, for example grim, OBS and xdg-desktop-portal-wlr (D37). A frame offers an shm buffer in XRGB8888. The core renders the output into it as on screen, without the cursor. Frames of both protocols wait for the next tick, one refresh later: each tick renders each output or toplevel once for all its frames, and a client has at most four frames waiting, so that no client can make the core render more than once per refresh and source. Newer tools use ext-image-copy-capture, which also captures a toplevel of ext-foreign-toplevel-list; the toplevel shows as screen.capture shows its node. Frames of both protocols fail while the session is locked. The renderer writes into shm buffers in shm.rs, which is the one place with unsafe code besides the GL calls in gl.rs.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text: The scene is a tree of nodes with stable ids. API lists the node properties. The order of the children sets the stacking order. The crate chora-scene holds the scene model (see Project structure).

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Each client names itself when it connects. The owner of a node is a client name, not a connection, so several choractl calls share their nodes.

  • Only the owner changes or removes a node.
  • A detached surface has no owner. The client that attaches it becomes its owner.
  • A child under a group does not change the group. The child keeps its own owner.
  • The removal of a group removes its descendants. Surfaces among them become detached.
  • When the last connection of a name closes, the core removes the nodes of that name. Its surfaces become detached. A client that connects with keep_nodes, for example choractl, keeps its nodes.

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text:
All outputs show one logical scene. Each output has a camera: a transform from scene coordinates to the logical coordinates of the output. The output scale then gives the pixels.

  • The default camera follows the output layout of wlr-output-management. An output at position (x, y) shows the scene area from (x, y) with the logical size of the output. Scene and layout coordinates then agree.
  • The camera command replaces the default, for example to pan or zoom. A camera is a 2D translation of at most 10^7 and a scale from 1/64 to 64. It ignores the z axis, so a uniform scale such as {"scale": 1.5} works. The first client that sets the camera of an output owns it. When the owner disconnects, the output gets its default camera back, unless the owner keeps its nodes with keep_nodes. The reset restores all default cameras.
  • Two outputs side by side get two adjacent default cameras. A window across two outputs then needs no special case.

docs.title: Output configuration
docs.text: The core implements wlr-output-management (D27), so kanshi and wlr-randr configure the outputs. Every output of the backend is a head of the protocol, also while it is off. A head can get a mode, a position, a transform and a scale, or turn off. The core tests a configuration as a whole before it applies it. If one part fails, the core changes nothing and answers failed. One output must stay on. After a change, the core places the layer surfaces again and announces the outputs to plugins (see API). On winit, the window decides the mode, and the output cannot turn off. No backend has adaptive sync.

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
The core uses Smithay's GLES renderer through Smithay's own renderer traits. Custom shaders give blur, rounded corners, shadows, color effects and transitions. niri shows what this approach can do. An effect is a GLSL ES fragment shader that a node names; the node becomes a layer, and each effect is one pass over its texture. The core compiles a shader when a transaction names it, rejects the transaction on an error, and compiles it again when the file changes. Shader nodes that draw without a texture, and uniforms that name other nodes as textures, come later.

Transforms are 4x4 matrices, so 3D effects need no API change. A node with a size and a mesh, or with a transform that is not a plain 2D translation and scale, is a layer: the core renders it with its descendants into a texture of its size, and then draws the texture through the mesh, or a quad, with the full transform of the node and the camera. The vertices go to the GPU in homogeneous coordinates, so textures map correctly under perspective. Wobbly windows move the points of a mesh, a magic lamp animates them, and a desktop cube turns layers in 3D. A layer has no depth test: the order of the siblings decides what is in front, and a plugin hides the faces that turn away. Pointer input reaches the nodes of a layer only where its transform is a plain 2D one.

Damage tracking keeps the GPU load low. Each shader declares if it is static or animated, and effects expand the damage area. A fullscreen surface without effects goes to direct scanout.

docs.title: IPC socket
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line, on a Unix socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora/. The socket has the name of the Wayland display, for example wayland-1.sock. The core exports the path as CHORA_SOCKET. calloop serves the socket in the event loop of the core, so no thread handoff is necessary. Events are JSON-RPC notifications on the same connection.

When a client closes its side of the connection, the core still answers the requests that arrived, also those of waiting transactions. Then it closes the connection.

Limits keep a buggy client from exhausting the core:

Limit Value Effect connections 128 the core refuses new connections time until hello 5 s the core closes the connection line length 1 MiB the core closes the connection output buffer of a connection 8 MiB the core closes the connection waiting transactions of a connection 16 the core rejects the transaction groups and rects in the scene 16,384 the core rejects the create cameras 64 the core rejects the camera

A plugin can export methods, for example tiling.set_layout. The core forwards a method call to the plugin as an event and returns the answer to the caller. A call without an answer fails after 10 s. An agent then asks the window manager for a change instead of fighting it (see API).

docs.title: choractl and the MCP bridge
docs.text: choractl is the CLI for the coordinator. It loads views and starts their plugins. choractl mcp serves the API as MCP tools over stdio, with tools for whole tasks such as describe_screen (see API). MCP stays out of the core, so the MCP side can change without a change to the compositor.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction is a batch of commands. The core applies it as one unit.

Some commands need a client round trip. A resize sends a configure event, and the client must answer with a new buffer. The core therefore holds the transaction until all affected clients commit, or until a deadline of 150 ms passes. Then the core shows all changes in the same frame (D22). Until then, a commit blocker holds each answer, so no new buffer shows early, at the old place.

A surface that misses the deadline is late. No transaction waits for it until it commits a buffer for its newest configure. A hung client thus delays the queue once, not once per transaction.

docs.title: Frame flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Backend
    participant C as Core
    participant R as Renderer
    B->>C: vblank
    C->>C: apply the transactions that are ready
    C->>C: advance the running animations
    C->>R: render the damaged parts of each camera
    R-->>B: page flip

docs.title: Input flow
docs.text:
1. libinput sends an event to the core.
  2. The safety layer checks its fixed bindings first.
  3. The plugins that grabbed the key or the pointer get the event. A plugin consumes the event or lets it pass.
  4. The focused surface gets each event that no plugin consumed. Pointer events go to the topmost node under the cursor that accepts input. The inverse of the camera maps the cursor to scene coordinates.

Plugins set the focus. The core changes it in three cases only:

  • The emergency reset focuses the first surface.
  • A click on a surface without an owner focuses it.
  • A surface that becomes detached loses the focus.

The core still implements the protocol mechanisms around focus: popup grabs, the keyboard interactivity of wlr-layer-shell and ext-session-lock, the locks and confinements of pointer-constraints, and text-input with input-method. Activation requests of xdg-activation and of taskbars go to plugins as surface.requested. A layer surface that takes the keyboard exclusively, for example a launcher, has it from its first commit until it goes away, and it ends a popup grab. A click gives the keyboard to a layer surface that accepts it on demand, until the next click elsewhere. A popup grabs the input only with the serial of the press that opened it.

docs.title: Safety layer
docs.text:
The safety layer is the only built-in behavior (see Vision). No plugin and no IPC client can change it.

  • Fixed bindings (D23). Injected input never triggers them; see Input injection.
  • SIGUSR1 starts the emergency reset too, for example from a text console when the keyboard no longer reaches the compositor.
  • Emergency reset. The core disconnects all plugins, revokes all grants, removes all effects, restores the default cameras and puts all surfaces in a simple grid. This grid is the one layout in the core. It is hardcoded, so a broken configuration cannot break it. The reset also changes the focus (see Input flow).
  • Session lock. The core enforces ext-session-lock. One client owns the lock; other clients cannot lock or unlock while it lives. While the session is locked, each output shows only its lock surface, or black. Only the lock client gets input; popup and pointer grabs end, and plugin grabs pause; a keyboard grab, for example of an input method, ends before each key. The core confirms the lock after each output showed a frame that it rendered under this lock. When the lock client crashes, the session stays locked, and only then can a new lock client take over.
  • Watchdog. When frames take longer to render than a refresh of their output for two seconds, the core removes the effects, the meshes and the shaders of shader nodes, and sends effects.dropped. When they stay slow for two more seconds, it starts the emergency reset, which disconnects the plugins.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Version 1 trusts every client of the same user (D33):

  • Unsandboxed Wayland clients get all protocols, as in sway. So any client can, for example, take the keyboard as an input method, or configure the outputs.
  • A sandbox such as Flatpak connects its apps through a socket of wp-security-context-v1. Those clients do not see the privileged protocols: the layer shell, the session lock, the input method, both foreign toplevel protocols, output management, both screencopy protocols with their sources, and the security context manager itself.
  • The IPC methods input.inject, screen.capture and process.spawn need a grant of the user for the client name: choractl grant NAME CAPABILITY (D40, D42). A grant protects against mistakes of agents. It is no barrier against hostile code of the same user. The emergency reset revokes all grants.
  • screen.capture, input.inject, process.spawn and plugins.restart fail while the session is locked.

docs.title: Sessions and flavors
docs.text:
• The session file chora.desktop runs chora-session tiling. The script imports the environment of the login into the systemd user manager and starts the user service chora@tiling.service. It waits until chora ends, and then stops the units of the graphical session.
  • Without XKB_DEFAULT_LAYOUT, chora-session takes the keyboard layout of the system from localectl.
  • chora@.service runs chora -- chora-flavor <name> as part of graphical-session.target. It drops WAYLAND_DISPLAY and DISPLAY that an earlier session left in the user manager, which would make chora run nested.
  • chora-flavor <name> imports WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET into the systemd user manager, and DISPLAY when xwayland-satellite is installed. It links the units of the flavor until the next boot, tells systemd that chora is ready, and starts the target of the flavor. Units of the flavor then find the compositor and the IPC socket. The script is not for nested use: the variables would reach the units of the host session.
  • The tiling flavor starts chora-tiling, waybar if it is installed, and xwayland-satellite on a free X11 display for X11 programs (D26).
  • A derived secureblue image installs the package (D10, D14).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Views are YAML files in git, and an agent can read and write them. A strict schema validates each file. It rejects unknown keys and catches the YAML traps, for example no read as false.

The core reads no configuration file. It runs one startup command (D30), for example chora-flavor, which starts the systemd target of a flavor:

chora -- chora-flavor tiling

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
~/.config/chora/
├── views/      # one file per view
├── flavors/    # bundles of views, plugins and services
├── plugins/    # plugin manifests
└── shaders/    # GLSL ES shaders

The directory is a git repository. It contains no secrets. The package installs the reference flavors to /usr/share/chora/.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
A view is a part of the scene and the plugins that drive it (D35):

# ~/.config/chora/views/work.yaml
name: work
plugins:
- name: tiling
  config: {layout: columns, gap: 12}
scene:
- id: work-corner
  kind: group
  props:
    transform: {translate: [1800, 20]}
- id: work-badge
  kind: rect
  parent: work-corner
  props:
    size: [100, 30]
    color: [0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0]
  • choractl view load work starts each plugin of the view that does not run yet, with the exec of its manifest, and waits up to 10 s until it connects. It passes each config to the method that the manifest names in configure. Then it applies the nodes of the view as one transaction.
  • The client view-work owns the nodes. A second load replaces them, choractl view unload work removes them.
  • choractl view save work writes the nodes of view-work as they are now, with the plugins of the file that was there, to ~/.config/chora/views/work.yaml, or to --file PATH. A plugin or an agent changes the nodes as view-work, for example choractl --name view-work apply.
  • A node has an id, a kind (group, rect or image), a parent (the root by default) and its props as in a create command.
  • A name has letters, digits, _, - and ., but no . first, so that its file stays in its directory. The file NAME.yaml must name the same view.
  • choractl view load also takes the path of a YAML file; the MCP tools take names only.
  • A plugin that a view starts gets no stdin and no stdout of choractl, which carry MCP under choractl mcp.

choractl looks for NAME.yaml in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/chora/views/ first (~/.config/chora/views/ by default), and then in /usr/share/chora/views/.

docs.title: Strict YAML
docs.text: choractl reads views and manifests with serde-saphyr (D41). Unknown keys, duplicate keys and unknown tags are errors. Only true and false are booleans, so no stays the string no.

docs.title: Plugin manifests
docs.text:
A manifest tells choractl how to start and how to configure a plugin. It lives in plugins/NAME.yaml of the same directories:

# /usr/share/chora/plugins/tiling.yaml
name: tiling
exec: chora-tiling
configure: set_layout
description: Tiles the windows as master and stack, columns or rows.
Key Meaning name the client name of the plugin exec the shell command that starts it configure the exported method that takes the config of a view; a view without config needs none description what the plugin does

The package installs the manifest of chora-tiling.

docs.title: Flavors
docs.text:
A flavor is a directory with views, plugin manifests and services, plus a systemd user target chora-<name>.target. chora-flavor <name> looks for the directory in ~/.config/chora/flavors/ first and then in /usr/share/chora/flavors/. It imports WAYLAND_DISPLAY, CHORA_SOCKET and the X11 DISPLAY of xwayland-satellite into the systemd user manager, so that every unit of the flavor starts with them. It links the units of the directory, and starts the target. The target starts the services and the plugins. systemd handles start, restart and order, so chora needs no service manager.

The package installs the tiling flavor:

/usr/share/chora/flavors/tiling/
├── chora-tiling.target              # wants the three units below
├── chora-tiling-wm.service          # chora-tiling
└── chora-tiling-xwayland.service    # xwayland-satellite, if installed

The target also wants waybar.service, which the waybar package installs. A copy of the directory in ~/.config/chora/flavors/tiling/ replaces it.

docs.title: The XP flavor
docs.text:
The XP flavor is the showroom of milestone M3 (D39): a stacking desktop in the style of Windows XP. It is a demo, not a daily driver.

/usr/share/chora/flavors/xp/
├── chora-xp.target              # wants the two units below
├── chora-xp-wm.service          # chora-xp
├── chora-xp-xwayland.service    # xwayland-satellite, if installed
└── theme/                       # SVG files, fonts, wallpaper and cursors

The session "chora (Windows XP)" on the login screen starts it with the XP cursors, which the package installs to /usr/share/icons/ModernXP. theme/README.md lists the source and the license of every file of the theme.

chora-xp draws everything as image nodes. It rasterizes the SVG files of the theme with resvg into PNG files in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora-xp/, and renders each picture once:

  • a frame around each window, with its title and the minimize, maximize and close buttons; a window that draws its own frame, as GTK programs do, gets none;
  • a taskbar at the bottom of the work area of each output, with the start button, one button per window of the current desktop, four desktop buttons and a clock;
  • the start menu with the user name, programs, places, Log Off and Turn Off Computer;
  • the wallpaper Bløff below everything.

A click on a window raises and focuses it. A drag of a title bar moves the window, and a double click maximizes it. A maximized window fills the work area above the taskbar. A click on a task button shows or minimizes its window. Buttons light up under the pointer, and so do the entries of the start menu. Log Off asks every window to close. Turn Off Computer ends chora-xp; it shuts nothing down.

The effects of M3 run in the plugin, which computes their meshes and transforms at 60 Hz:

  • Wobbly windows. A dragged window bends like jelly: the point under the pointer follows it, the far side lags behind, and after the release the window shakes until it settles.
  • Magic lamp. Minimize pours the window into its task button, and a click on the button pours it out again.
  • Desktop cube. Four desktops sit on the faces of a cube. A turn shows the cube in perspective, and the windows fly off their faces and land again. The taskbar lists the windows of the current desktop.

If frames get too slow, the core drops the effects; chora-xp then goes without them for 15 seconds.

Binding Action Alt+F4 close the focused window Super+e start the terminal Ctrl+Alt+Left, Ctrl+Alt+Right turn the cube to the previous or next desktop Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Left, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Right turn the cube and take the focused window along a desktop button 1 to 4 turn the cube to that desktop

The safety layer keeps only Ctrl+Alt with BackSpace, Escape and F1 to F12, so the cube takes Ctrl+Alt with the arrows. When another client holds these bindings, Super+Ctrl with the arrows stands in.

Option Default Meaning --theme DIR /usr/share/chora/flavors/xp/theme, or CHORA_XP_THEME the theme directory --terminal CMD foot the terminal of the start menu and of Super+e --launcher CMD fuzzel All Programs and Run in the start menu --program TITLE=CMD another program in the start menu; repeat for more --clock FORMAT %-I:%M %p the clock, in the format of strftime --wallpaper FILE Bløff a PNG or SVG file --slow-motion FACTOR 1 stretch the magic lamp and the cube, to show them slowly

To try the flavor from a source tree, start it nested:

cargo build --workspace
target/debug/chora -- target/debug/chora-xp --theme flavors/xp/theme

flavors/agentic/
├── chora-agentic.target
├── views/       # morning, analysis, writing, coding
├── plugins/     # canvas layout, keybindings
└── services/    # Quadlet units: speech, browser in app mode

docs.title: Services
docs.text: A service runs as a Quadlet unit with Podman, or in distrobox. It connects to the IPC socket, appears as a Wayland client, or both. A container mounts $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora/ (in Quadlet: %t/chora) and gets CHORA_SOCKET from the environment of the unit.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: The decision log. Nothing here is final. Every entry can come back for review.

docs.title: Principles and scope
docs.text: # Decision Reason D1 Rust and Smithay for the core Smithay is a library without policy, proven in niri and cosmic-comp. Rust is safe when agents change the system live. D2 Everything is a plugin Maximum flexibility and a small core. D3 An experimentation platform first, then a stable, feature-complete core, then testing A small core gives stability. D4 Reuse before writing; check alternatives for every decision Little code to maintain. D5 One vocabulary, defined in the Glossary One language for people and agents. D6 Inventory and agent memory form a separate layer, not part of the core The platform stays neutral. D7 The name is chora, always in lowercase See Vision. D8 The core is GPL-3.0-or-later; code under GPL-3.0-only stays out The core can then reuse code from Pinnacle and niri. D9 English for code and documentation The documentation is public.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text: # Decision Reason D10 Fedora 44 and secureblue as host; a derived image offers chora as an additional session The system and the image tooling of the author. D11 AMD and Intel GPUs first, NVIDIA later The hardware of the author. Mesa drivers need no special paths. D12 Services run as Quadlet units with Podman or in distrobox Isolation. systemd handles start, restart and order. D13 The coordinator is the user first, later an agent with special permissions A gradual path to control by agents. D14 Releases are RPM packages for Fedora 44, attached with SHA256 sums to a GitHub release; a v* tag starts the release; versions below 1.0 are pre-releases dnf5 install <url> installs them by hand and in the image build.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: # Decision Reason D15 Build on Smithay; copy from Pinnacle, niri and anvil; no fork A fork of Pinnacle keeps less than half of its code. See Alternatives. D16 Pin a Smithay git revision No Smithay release since 0.7.0. All major users track git. D17 GLES renderer and GLSL shaders through Smithay's renderer traits Proven in niri. No Smithay compositor uses wgpu. D18 Five node kinds: group, surface, rect, image, shader Text and widgets come from Wayland clients. An image node shows a PNG asset, for example a window border, without a client per window. A shader can read another node as a texture. D19 Transforms are 4x4 matrices; the first milestones test 2D cases only 3D effects need no API change later. D20 One logical scene; each output shows it through a camera Pan, zoom and the infinite canvas need no extra mechanism. D21 The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces; toplevels wait for a plugin The protocols define these positions. Smithay implements them. D22 A transaction completes when all affected clients commit, or after a deadline A resize needs a client round trip. D23 A hardcoded safety layer with fixed bindings: Ctrl+Alt+Backspace quits, Ctrl+Alt+Escape resets, Ctrl+Alt+F1 to F12 switch the VT; SIGUSR1 resets too A recovery path must not depend on a file that an agent can break. D24 Shaders declare static or animated; fullscreen surfaces without effects use direct scanout Damage tracking and battery life. D25 No undo history and no plugin state store in the core A destroyed client cannot come back. The reset and the views in git cover recovery. The scene holds all state. D26 Xwayland through xwayland-satellite Keeps the core small. D27 Output configuration through wlr-output-management kanshi and wlr-randr exist.

docs.title: Plugins and API
docs.text: # Decision Reason D28 Plugins are IPC clients; the core offers animate; in-process WASM plugins come only after a measurement shows the need Agents work in seconds, not frames. One mechanism, any language, crash isolation by the OS. The M3 measurement (tests/ipc-bench.sh, nested, software rendering) shows no need yet: a transaction with a mesh of 8x8 cells takes 0.17 ms in the median and 3.6 ms at the 99th percentile, well inside a 60 Hz frame. D29 JSON-RPC 2.0 with one message per line on a Unix socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora/; the core serves it from the calloop event loop No extra runtime and no thread handoff. A container mounts the directory. D30 The core starts one startup command with WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET set The startup command starts the plugins, or a systemd target. D31 A client names itself when it connects; the owner of a node is a client name; only the owner changes a node; plugins export methods An agent asks the window manager instead of fighting it. D32 Selectors work in queries only; a query returns all current matches No window rules in the core. Predictable results for agents. D33 Version 1 trusts the clients of the same user; wp-security-context-v1 hides privileged protocols from sandboxed clients; the IPC methods input.inject and screen.capture need a grant of the user The grant protects against mistakes of agents. It is no barrier against hostile code of the same user. D34 MCP outside the core: choractl mcp over stdio, with tools for whole tasks The core stays free of MCP. D35 The core reads no configuration; choractl loads YAML views; a flavor is a directory with a systemd target; the configuration holds no secrets Policy and service management do not belong in the core. D36 Three crates to start: chora-scene, chora, choractl; reference plugins in plugins/ A crate comes when a second consumer needs it.

docs.title: Tools around the core
docs.text: # Decision Reason D37 Screen sharing through xdg-desktop-portal-wlr first No code. A portal backend of its own is in the Idea backlog. D38 HTML content from agents runs in a browser in app mode, as a service No code. chora places toplevels anywhere. D39 The first showcase is a flavor in the style of Windows XP with wobbly windows, a magic lamp minimize and a 3D desktop cube; it comes right after M2, before the agent interface It proves that the scene model carries classic mouse-driven desktops and their effects. The assets come from kde-plasma-winxp-launcher and keep their licenses; the GPL-3.0-only artwork of Exposé and modernXP is data of the flavor that the plugin reads, not code of the core (D8). It is a demo, not a daily driver. D40 The user grants input.inject and screen.capture with choractl grant NAME CAPABILITY, per client name, until the session ends or choractl revoke; the emergency reset revokes all grants; choractl mcp has no tool for grants The core draws no text, so a dialog is no option. An agent that uses the MCP bridge cannot grant itself by mistake. D41 choractl reads YAML with serde-saphyr: strict booleans, errors on unknown and duplicate keys and on unknown tags serde_yaml is archived and serde_yml is unsound. serde-saphyr is maintained, pure Rust and panic-free, and limits the work of a document (open question 1). D42 process.spawn starts programs as the user behind a grant of its own, which the user gives with choractl grant NAME process.spawn and the reset revokes; an allowlist of argv patterns that comes with the grant may narrow it later An agent with this grant can run anything, as with a shell, so it is never part of another grant. The allowlist keeps the core free of configuration files (D35).

Roadmap assigns each protocol to a milestone.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The shared vocabulary of chora. Code, docs and prompts to agents use these terms and no synonyms.

Term Meaning Core The compositor process chora. It handles the Wayland protocols, the backends (DRM/KMS, libinput), the scene, the renderer, the input routing, the IPC socket and the safety layer. It contains no policy. Scene The tree of nodes that the core renders every frame. It is the single source of truth for the screen content. Node One element of the scene. The kinds are group, surface, rect, image and shader. Every node has an id, an owner, a transform, an opacity and optional effects. Group A node that contains other nodes. It applies a transform, a clip, an opacity and optional effects to its children. Canvas A group that serves as a working area: a workspace, a desktop or an infinite zoomable plane. Surface A node that shows a Wayland client: an application window, a layer-shell widget or a browser window. For the core, a surface is a texture source and an input target. Rect A colored rectangle with optional rounded corners and border. Shader A node that a fragment shader draws completely. A shader can read other nodes as textures. A shader can also be an effect. Effect A shader that changes how a node and its children look, for example blur or a color change. Every node can have effects. Camera The part of the scene that one output shows: a transform from scene coordinates to the logical coordinates of the output. Work area The part of the scene that an output shows, without the zones that panels and IPC clients reserve. Plugins place windows in it. Client A process on the IPC socket: a plugin, choractl or a service. A client names itself when it connects. Owner The client name that created or attached a node. Only the owner changes the node. Toplevel A surface with the role of an application window (xdg_toplevel). Other roles are layer surfaces and popups. Detached The state of a surface node without a parent. A detached surface is not visible. View A declarative arrangement: nodes, the plugins that drive them, and their configuration. A view is a YAML file in git. The user or an agent changes it live. Plugin A client that reacts to events, changes the scene and can export methods. A window manager, a layout, an animation set and a keybinding set are plugins. Service A process in a container, outside the core. Examples are speech recognition, a local LLM and a development environment. Flavor A preconfigured bundle of views, plugins and services, for example "classic", "tiling" or "agentic". Coordinator The party that installs and connects plugins, services and flavors. First the user, later an agent with special permissions. Inventory A local, git-versioned store of reusable elements (views, plugins, widgets). It belongs to the opinionated layer above chora, not to the core. Command A request to change the scene, for example create or update. Event A message from the core about a change, for example surface.created. Selector An expression that finds nodes by id, attribute or meta data, for example app_id:firefox. Transaction A batch of commands that the core applies as one unit. If one command fails, the core applies none of them. Grant A permission of the user for one client name to use input.inject, screen.capture or process.spawn. Safety layer The only built-in behavior of the core: fixed bindings, emergency reset, session lock, watchdog.

docs.title: Idea backlog
docs.text: All ideas that are not decisions yet. An idea moves to Decisions or leaves the list.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text:
• Voice as the main channel to an agent: speech to text in, text to speech out, with a robust push-to-talk or wake-word mechanism.
  • A morning view: greeting, current tasks, sorted email, and a day plan that user and agent prioritize together.
  • A view for each task, built on demand: data analysis with data, plots and interactive exploration; email; web research; coding.
  • Live changes by voice: resize, rearrange, highlight, dim, switch views.
  • Views that fit the task and the taste of the user. The agent learns the layout preferences of the user.

docs.title: Visuals
docs.text:
• Effects like in Hyprland and Compiz: blur, shadows, rounded corners, an overview, transitions. Wobbly windows, the magic lamp and the cube are part of M3 (D39).
  • An infinite zoomable canvas through cameras.
  • Surfaces as 3D objects.
  • Pixel-perfect copies of existing desktops as flavors, for example KDE Plasma. The XP showroom of M3 is the first (D39). They prove the flexibility. They are not a goal.

docs.title: Agents and the ecosystem around chora
docs.text:
• An inventory: a local, git-versioned store of reusable elements. Code for one-time use goes away, useful code stays.
  • Agent memory in the home directory.
  • Demiurge as the name of the coordinating agent. In Plato, the demiurge shapes the forms in the chora.

docs.title: Core extensions
docs.text:
• In-process WASM plugins on wasmtime with the Component Model, for effects that need code in every frame, for example wobbly windows. Only after a measurement shows the need (D28).
  • A portal backend of its own, so that screen sharing can share a group or a canvas instead of a whole output or window.
  • Restricted IPC sockets for containers: a socket that only offers a subset of the API to the clients behind it.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• A local inference engine (LLM) in a container.
  • Speech services (whisper, piper).
  • Development environments with special configurations (distrobox).
  • A dedicated webview host on gtk4-layer-shell, if a browser in app mode is too slow, too heavy or cannot be transparent.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
• Flavors as installable bundles: classic, tiling, agentic.
  • A later registry for plugins and flavors, possibly as OCI artifacts. OCI fits the container world of the host.
  • A Copr repository, so that dnf updates chora like every other package.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
The layout of this repository: one Cargo workspace with as few crates as possible. A module moves into its own crate only when a second consumer needs it.

chora/
├── crates/
│   ├── chora-scene/   # scene model, commands, events, selectors, IPC types and client; no Smithay
│   ├── chora/         # the compositor: Smithay, backends, renderer, input, safety, IPC
│   └── choractl/      # CLI over the IPC socket; `choractl mcp` is the MCP bridge
├── plugins/
│   ├── chora-tiling/  # reference plugin: master and stack, columns, rows, keybindings
│   └── chora-xp/      # stacking window manager in the style of Windows XP
├── flavors/           # systemd units of the flavors; the theme of the XP flavor
├── dist/              # RPM build script, Fedora build requirements, session files
├── tests/             # end-to-end tests in a headless sway
├── deny.toml          # cargo-deny: allowed licenses, advisories
├── docs/              # this documentation (MkDocs)
├── mkdocs.yml
└── Cargo.toml         # workspace, lints

docs.title: Reasons for this split
docs.text:
• chora-scene has no Smithay dependency. Tests of the data model and the transaction logic need no GPU and no compositor. The core, choractl and plugins share this one definition of the API.
  • Reference plugins live in this repository first, as workspace members. They keep the API honest. They can move out when the API is stable.
  • The build generates the schemas from the Rust types. The repository does not contain them. Docs, validation and agents then see the same contract.
