docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Each milestone has a goal, a scope and an exit criterion. A milestone is done when its exit criterion holds. After M4 the core is feature complete, and testing starts (D3). M5 and M6 build on the core.

docs.title: M0: Workspace and tooling
docs.text:
Goal: the first line of Rust meets all guards, and a tag produces a package.

  • Cargo workspace with chora-scene, chora, choractl and the reference plugins in plugins/ (D36).
  • Workspace lints: clippy pedantic, cognitive_complexity and excessive_nesting; unsafe_code denied. clippy.toml sets the limits.
  • CI: build and cargo test in a Fedora 44 container; cargo-deny for the licenses and advisories of the dependencies.
  • A pre-commit hook that rejects files with a GPL-3.0-only header (D8).
  • Dependabot for Cargo.
  • commitizen for version bumps and the changelog.
  • A release workflow: a v* tag builds the RPM in Fedora 44 and attaches it with its SHA256 sum to a GitHub pre-release (D14).

Exit: CI is green. The RPM of a test build installs in a Fedora 44 container, and chora --version runs there.

docs.title: M1: Nested proof of concept
docs.text:
Goal: the smallest proof of the concept, inside an existing session.

  • winit backend on a pinned Smithay revision (D16).
  • Protocols: xdg-shell with popups, subsurfaces, xdg-decoration, linux-dmabuf, viewporter, xdg-output, data device and primary-selection.
  • Scene with group, surface and rect nodes, 2D transforms (D18, D19).
  • Transactions that wait for client commits (D22).
  • IPC socket (D29) with hello, scene.query, scene.apply, events.subscribe, input.grab and output.list.
  • Ownership (D31).
  • The startup command (D30).
  • Safety layer: quit and emergency reset (D23).
  • choractl with query, apply, events and outputs.
  • chora-tiling: a reference plugin with a master and stack layout and keybindings to start a terminal, close a window and move the focus.

Exit: an automated test in a headless sway passes:

  1. chora -- chora-tiling starts nested.
  2. Three foot windows appear without overlap. scene.query and a screenshot confirm the layout.
  3. After kill of chora-tiling, chora still runs, and the three surfaces are detached.
  4. The emergency reset puts the three surfaces in the grid. The test sends SIGUSR1, because synthetic keys do not reach a nested compositor.

The test, tests/nested.sh, also checks fixed regressions.

docs.title: M2: Session on real hardware
docs.text:
Goal: chora runs as a login session on AMD and Intel (D11).

  • udev, DRM/KMS, libinput and libseat backends; the VT switch bindings.
  • Several outputs, cameras (D20) and the camera command; wlr-output-management (D27).
  • Commit blockers, as in niri and Pinnacle, so that the new buffers of a transaction appear in the same frame.
  • Protocols: cursor-shape, presentation-time, wlr-layer-shell, ext-session-lock, ext-idle-notify, idle-inhibit, text-input, input-method, pointer-constraints, relative-pointer, ext-foreign-toplevel-list, wlr-foreign-toplevel-management, xdg-activation, fractional-scale.
  • xwayland-satellite (D26).
  • chora.desktop, chora-flavor and a tiling flavor with a systemd target.

Exit:

  1. Automated, nested: waybar, fuzzel and swaylock work.
  2. On the hardware of the author: a tiling session with bar and launcher runs for 8 hours on an AMD and on an Intel machine, without a crash or a restart of the core.

docs.title: M3: Effects and the XP showroom
docs.text:
Goal: the game-engine half of the idea, shown in a flavor in the style of Windows XP (D39). The flavor is a demo, not a daily driver.

  • Image nodes for assets, and shader nodes, effects and shaders that read nodes as textures (D18).
  • Rendering of a node into a texture, and a mesh that deforms that texture. Wobbly windows and the magic lamp minimize use the mesh.
  • Perspective for the 4x4 transforms, for a 3D desktop cube with flying windows. Layers have no depth test: the order of the siblings decides what is in front.
  • The animate command (D28).
  • GLSL hot reload; compile errors as transaction.rejected.
  • Damage tracking for static and animated shaders, direct scanout (D24).
  • The watchdog of the safety layer.
  • A measurement of the IPC round trip for effects in every frame. The result decides on in-process WASM plugins (D28).
  • An XP flavor: a stacking window manager with title bars, a taskbar and a start menu, with the assets of kde-plasma-winxp-launcher.

Exit:

  1. Automated, nested: the XP flavor starts. A screenshot shows the taskbar, the start button and two windows with title bars. A drag of a window deforms its mesh. A minimize runs the magic lamp. A key binding turns the desktop cube with four desktops.
  2. On the Intel machine at 60 Hz, four windows with blur and rounded corners and a 300 ms transition: presentation-time shows at least 99 percent of the frames on time over 60 seconds.

docs.title: M4: Agent interface
docs.text:
Goal: an agent sees and changes the screen.

  • Grants for input.inject and screen.capture (D33, D40).
  • ext-image-copy-capture and wlr-screencopy; xdg-desktop-portal-wlr for screen sharing (D37).
  • Plugin methods: methods.export and methods.call (D31).
  • choractl view load and choractl view save with YAML views (D35).
  • choractl mcp over stdio, with tools for whole tasks (D34).
  • wp-security-context-v1.

Exit: an automated test passes: an MCP client asks for "describe the screen", calls tiling.set_layout, and the next screenshot shows the new layout. The last step of tests/agent.sh checks it with tests/mcp-client.py in CI.

docs.title: M4.1: Agent feedback
docs.text:
Goal: an agent builds an interactive view in a few calls, from the feedback of the first real MCP sessions (issues #3 to #10).

  • Docs and code agree (#3): clip on all nodes, radius and border on rects, and the shader node kind with a uniform that names a node as texture (D18). A test parses every example of docs/api.md.
  • A camera takes a uniform scale of the short form (#4), and animates in the core with duration and easing (#10).
  • choractl mcp: item schemas for apply_commands and inject_input from the types of chora-scene (#5), and tools to subscribe to and wait for events (#7).
  • assets.put stores an image or a shader of a client in another namespace in a directory of the core, removed with the nodes of the client (#6).
  • output.reserve reduces the work area for the life of a connection (#8); the reserve of chora-tiling goes.
  • process.spawn starts a program with the environment of the startup command, behind its own grant (D42), and plugins.restart restarts a plugin of a view (#9).
  • Option: harden the grant with an allowlist, for example regular expressions over the argv. choractl grant reads the list from a file in ~/.config/chora/ and hands it to the core with the grant, since the core reads no configuration (D35); the core then refuses every other program.

Exit: an automated test passes: an MCP client uploads a shader, reserves a panel at the edge of the output, draws it as a rounded shader node with two buttons, and moves the camera with an animation when the user clicks a button, which the client learns from wait_events. The last step of tests/agent.sh checks it with tests/mcp-client.py panel in CI. The allowlist of the grant process.spawn stays an option.

docs.title: M5: Packaging
docs.text:
Goal: chora installs like every other desktop on the host.

  • A derived secureblue image with the chora package (D10, D14).
  • The tiling flavor in the image, and a classic flavor.
  • Services as Quadlet units (D12).

Exit: after an image update, the login screen offers chora. The tiling flavor starts, and one Quadlet service connects to the IPC socket.

docs.title: M6: Agentic flavor
docs.text:
Goal: the agentic workday scenario works end to end.

  • Speech services: whisper.cpp or faster-whisper, piper.
  • A browser in app mode as service for HTML content (D38).
  • A morning view and task views.
  • Task and email sources are MCP servers of the agent, outside chora.

Exit: the user says "show my tasks for today", and the agent opens a morning view with the tasks from an MCP source. Then the user says "open a view for the first task", and the agent opens a view with at least two surfaces.

docs.title: After M6
docs.text:
• Conformance tests with wlcs, as Pinnacle does.
  • Hardening and testing on the daily system.
  • Items from the Idea backlog.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Three scenarios test the concept and estimate the effort on top of the core. The estimates are rough. They assume that the core implements the common Wayland protocols (see Dependencies), so existing tools work unchanged.

docs.title: 1. Classic desktop
docs.text:
A Windows-like desktop with taskbar, start menu and overlapping windows, driven by mouse and keyboard. This is not the goal of chora, but it must be possible.

Part Source Effort Stacking window manager: move, resize, raise, focus, minimize plugin about 1000 to 2000 lines Window decorations: title bar, buttons plugin with rect and shader nodes, a decoration surface of the plugin, or client-side decorations small to medium Keybindings: Alt+Tab, Super key plugin small Taskbar, tray, clock existing shell: Quickshell, waybar, eww configuration Start menu, launcher fuzzel, wofi or a Quickshell widget configuration Wallpaper swaybg or swww configuration Pixel-perfect XP look theme assets, shaders, decorations much detail work, little difficulty

The taskbar needs the foreign-toplevel protocols to see the windows. The launcher and the bar need wlr-layer-shell.

Result: medium effort, almost all of it in one window manager plugin.

docs.title: 2. Keyboard-driven tiling
docs.text:
A Linux-style tiling workflow with workspaces. The user configures it.

Part Source Effort Tiling layout: master and stack, columns, scrolling plugin a few hundred lines Workspaces one group per workspace, switched by visibility or transform small Keybindings, focus movement plugin small Bar waybar or Quickshell configuration Animations the animate command of the core small

Result: low effort. This is a good first flavor to test the plugin API.

docs.title: 3. Agentic workday
docs.text:
This scenario is the core idea. A robust voice channel connects the user to an agent, and the agent arranges content for each task.

  1. Morning view. The agent greets the user and shows the current tasks. It sorts the email. User and agent plan and prioritize the day together.
  2. Task views. The agent builds a new canvas for each task and fills it. A data analysis gets prepared data, plots and interactive exploration. Email, web research and coding get their own views.
  3. Reuse. The inventory keeps useful elements in git for later use. The agent discards code for one-time use.
  4. Live change by voice. "Make the plot bigger." "Put the terminal next to the notebook." "Dim everything except the editor." The agent calls the methods of the window manager plugin for these changes.
Part Source Effort Scene access for the agent IPC socket and choractl mcp part of the API Speech in and out services: whisper.cpp or faster-whisper, piper integration The agent Claude Code or another MCP client, later a local LLM service integration Rich content: greeting, plots, email the agent writes HTML, a browser in app mode shows it as a surface generated content Data exploration Jupyter, marimo or a plot web app as surfaces existing tools One view per task YAML views that choractl loads, saves and changes live coordinator tool Inventory, memory opinionated layer above chora later

Result: the largest scenario, but mostly integration of existing parts. The core must supply scene queries and changes, screenshots and input injection. The agent needs screenshots to see the result of its changes.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
• The four node kinds cover all three scenarios.
  • Text, images and widgets do not need to live in the core. Existing shells, wallpaper tools and a browser in app mode supply them.
  • Two core features decide the success. The protocol coverage lets existing tools work. The API lets plugins and agents arrange everything.

docs.title: Vision and principles
docs.text: chora is the space where forms appear.

docs.title: The name
docs.text: Plato calls the space in which things come into being chora (χώρα). chora is neither form nor matter. It only gives the forms a place. The compositor works the same way: it has no content and no policy of its own. Plugins, clients and agents bring the forms.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A desktop decides the arrangement of the content: windows, panels, workspaces. chora takes this decision out of the compositor. chora is a programmable scene. It works more like a game engine than like a window manager. The core renders a scene of nodes every frame. One API changes the scene live.

The motivating use case is agentic interaction. The user talks to an agent, ideally by voice. The agent arranges the screen for the current task and for the taste of the user. Examples are a morning view, a data exploration view and a coding view. The agent changes the arrangement while the user works.

Agents are the motivation, not a requirement. The same scene can host a pixel-perfect Windows XP desktop, a keyboard-driven tiling setup or a KDE-like workflow. It can also host a kind of human-machine interaction that does not exist yet. chora ships none of them. chora makes all of them possible.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Everything is a plugin. The core has no policy: no layout, no focus model, no keybindings, no decorations, no defaults. The window manager is a plugin too. A core without plugins shows a black screen.
  2. Safety is the only built-in behavior. The core keeps an escape hatch that no plugin can override: VT switch, quit, and an emergency reset. Agents will write broken code live, so this exception is necessary.
  3. Lean core, fast stability. A small core reaches feature completeness fast. Then the project hardens it. Features grow in plugins, not in the core.
  4. Reuse before writing. Wayland protocol handling, rendering, widgets, shells and services already exist. chora connects these parts and writes only what is missing. Fixes go upstream. Every decision gets a check for existing alternatives.
  5. One API for every caller. Plugins, scripts, the CLI, services and agents use the same scene language. An agent can change everything that a user can configure, and it can change it live.
  6. Live and real time. Changes apply while the session runs. They need no restart and cause no noticeable latency.
  7. Declarative and versioned. The configuration is plain text in git: views in YAML, and flavors as bundles of files. A diff shows each change. An agent can read and write the files easily.
  8. Isolation by default. Plugins run as separate processes, services in containers. Input injection and screen capture through the API need a grant of the user (D33).

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Start as an experimentation platform. Reach a stable, feature-complete core fast, then start testing.
  • Run as an additional session on a Fedora host, next to the existing desktops. The concrete host is a derived secureblue image.
  • Add features as plugins and as services in containers.
  • Let a coordinator install and connect plugins and services. The first coordinator is the user. A later coordinator is an agent with special permissions that can also write new plugins and services.
  • Make it possible to rebuild any existing workflow, with effort, and to invent new ones.

docs.title: Non-goals for now
docs.text:
• A usable desktop out of the box. A flavor can supply one. The core never does.
  • Agent memory and a local inventory of reusable elements. These form a separate, opinionated layer on top of chora (see Idea backlog).
  • Distributions other than Fedora and secureblue, and GPUs other than AMD and Intel, until the core is stable.
